aaqParts.name: Research method
aaqParts.tip: Look for random assignment, manipulation of a variable, and control/experimental groups.
aaqParts.mistake: Calling an experiment a "correlational study" because it measured variables. Random assignment + a manipulated variable = experiment.

aaqParts.name: Research variable
aaqParts.tip: Scan the Method section for how the variable was actually measured or tested.
aaqParts.mistake: Giving a textbook definition instead of how THIS study measured it.

aaqParts.name: Statistic interpretation
aaqParts.tip: Always connect the number back to what it means for the research question.
aaqParts.mistake: Just restating the numbers ("the mean was 7.81") without saying which group did better and what that tells us.

aaqParts.name: Ethical guidelines
aaqParts.tip: Read the Method section carefully. Ethical practices are often described without being named.
aaqParts.mistake: Naming a guideline the researchers SHOULD have followed but that the article never describes.

aaqParts.name: Generalizability
aaqParts.tip: The demographic table is the key. Reference specific percentages from the participant data.
aaqParts.mistake: Saying "the study is (not) generalizable" without citing specific demographics (age, race, gender, location).

aaqParts.name: Argumentation
aaqParts.tip: Use specific numbers from the Results section and explicitly say whether they support or refute the hypothesis.
aaqParts.mistake: A conclusion with no specific data (1 pt), or data with no explanation of how it connects to the hypothesis (1 pt). You need both for 2.

ebqParts.label: A
ebqParts.name: Claim
ebqParts.q: Propose a specific and defensible claim based in psychological science that responds to the question.
ebqParts.tip: Take a clear position the sources can back up. "Should," "because," and "depends on" help make a claim specific.
ebqParts.mistake: A vague claim ("Social media affects teenagers") or one that just restates the question earns 0.

ebqParts.label: B(i)
ebqParts.name: Evidence #1
ebqParts.q: Support your claim using at least one piece of specific and relevant evidence from one of the sources.
ebqParts.tip: Pick specific data (numbers, groups, results) and cite it: "(Source 1)" or "According to Source 1…".
ebqParts.mistake: No citation, or a vague summary of a source instead of specific data.

ebqParts.label: B(ii)
ebqParts.name: Explain + apply
ebqParts.q: Explain how the evidence from Part B(i) supports your claim using a psychological perspective, theory, concept, or research finding learned in AP Psychology.
ebqParts.tip: Two moves: (1) say HOW the evidence supports your claim, (2) name a psych concept from class and use it to explain WHY the result happened.
ebqParts.mistake: Explaining the evidence without applying a concept (1 pt), or "applying" a term that comes from the sources (depression, sleep, screen time…).

ebqParts.label: C(i)
ebqParts.name: Evidence #2
ebqParts.q: Support your claim using an additional piece of specific and relevant evidence from a different source than the one that you used to support your claim in Part B(i).
ebqParts.tip: Use a DIFFERENT source than Part B. Plan which two sources you will use during the reading period.
ebqParts.mistake: Using the same source as Part B(i): it earns 0 even if the evidence is good.

ebqParts.label: C(ii)
ebqParts.name: Explain + apply
ebqParts.q: Explain how the evidence from Part C(i) supports your claim using a different psychological perspective, theory, concept, or research finding learned in AP Psychology than the one that you used in Part B(ii).
ebqParts.tip: Use a DIFFERENT concept than Part B(ii). Plan two concepts before you start writing.
ebqParts.mistake: Reusing the concept from B(ii) caps this part at 1 point.

frq.aaqRubric:
AP Psychology Article Analysis Question (AAQ) rubric. Parts A-E are worth 1 point each; Part F is worth 2 points.
A (Research method, task verb IDENTIFY): earn the point for naming the correct research method (experiment, correlational study, case study, naturalistic observation, meta-analysis, etc.). Random assignment + a manipulated variable = experiment. No explanation is required.
B (Research variable, STATE): earn the point for the operational definition used IN THIS STUDY: how the researchers actually measured or manipulated the variable, with measurable specifics from the Method. A general textbook definition earns 0.
C (Statistic interpretation, DESCRIBE): earn the point for saying what the statistic means for the study (which group did better / direction and meaning of the relationship) and connecting it to what was investigated. Only restating the numbers earns 0.
D (Ethical guidelines, IDENTIFY + DESCRIBE): earn the point only if the student names a specific ethical guideline that the article actually describes AND describes how the researchers applied it, with evidence from the article. A guideline not described in the article earns 0.
E (Generalizability, EXPLAIN): earn the point for a claim about whether the findings generalize, naming a specific population, AND citing specific participant demographics from the study (percentages, ages, location, etc.). No specific demographics = 0.
F (Argumentation, EXPLAIN): point 1 for citing a specific result (data) from the study; point 2 for an accurate explanation of how that result supports or refutes the hypothesis/claim. Claiming a correlational or observational study proves causation is NOT accurate.
Be fair like a real AP reader: accept any correct wording, do not require the model answer's exact words, ignore spelling, and do not award points for vague or incorrect answers.
frq.ebqRubric:
AP Psychology Evidence-Based Question (EBQ) rubric, 7 points.
A (Claim, 1 pt, PROPOSE): a specific, defensible claim based in psychological science that responds to the question. Vague claims ("Social media affects teenagers") or restatements of the question earn 0.
B(i) (Evidence #1, 1 pt, SUPPORT): specific, relevant evidence from ONE source that supports the claim, with a citation such as "(Source 1)" or "According to Source 1". No citation = 0. Vague summaries = 0.
B(ii) (Explain + apply, 2 pts): point 1 for explaining how the B(i) evidence supports the claim; point 2 for ALSO applying a psychological perspective, theory, concept, or research finding learned in AP Psychology (e.g., social comparison theory, operant conditioning, circadian rhythm, memory consolidation, Erikson, Piaget, neuroplasticity, prefrontal cortex). Terms that come from the sources themselves (e.g., depression, well-being, sleep, screen time), "statistically significant," and vague popular ideas do NOT count as applied concepts. Opinion only = 0.
C(i) (Evidence #2, 1 pt): like B(i) but from a DIFFERENT source than B(i). Same source as B(i) = 0.
C(ii) (Explain + apply, 2 pts): like B(ii) but with a DIFFERENT concept than B(ii). Reusing B(ii)'s concept caps C(ii) at 1.
Be fair like a real AP reader: accept any correct wording, ignore spelling, and do not award points for vague or incorrect answers. Evidence must actually support the student's claim.

guide.p: 7 points · 25 minutes (including a 10-minute reading period) · 1 summarized peer-reviewed article. Parts A–E are 1 point each; Part F is 2.

Read the Method section carefully. Ethical practices are often described without being named.
The demographic table is the key. Reference specific percentages from the participant data.

rows: Identify
Name it. No explanation needed. One sentence is enough.
Describe
Give the relevant characteristics: what it is and what it shows. You don't need to explain why.
Explain
The big one: HOW or WHY something happens, with evidence and reasoning.

guide.p: You can't write, but you CAN annotate. 1) First read (3–4 min): what were they studying, what did they find? 2) Annotate (4–5 min): method, IV and DV, operational definitions, statistics, ethical practices, demographics. 3) Preview the six questions (1–2 min).

Reading 10 min · Parts A–D about 7 min (~1.5 each) · Parts E–F about 8 min (3–4 each). Never spend more than 2 minutes on a 1-point part. Save 3–4 minutes for Part F. If you finish early, recheck E and F first: that's where most points are lost.

Label every part (A, B, C…). Answer what's asked: match the task verb. Use psych terminology ("randomly assigned to experimental and control conditions," not "split into groups"). Quote the article: numbers, percentages, details.

a-sleep.title: Sleep Deprivation and Memory for Word Lists
a-sleep.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-sleep.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: Researchers wanted to know whether losing a night of sleep affects how well people remember new information. They hypothesized that sleep deprivation impairs memory.
120 undergraduate students from a single university in Ohio took part in exchange for course credit. Participants were 18 to 22 years old (mean age 19.6). See the table for demographics.

Participants were randomly assigned to one of two groups. The sleep-deprived group stayed awake all night in the sleep lab, monitored by research assistants. The rested group slept for 8 hours in the same lab. The next morning, every participant studied a list of 40 words for 5 minutes and then had 3 minutes to write down as many of the words as they could remember. Memory recall was measured as the number of words correctly written down. Before the study, every participant read and signed a consent form that explained they might be asked to stay awake all night. They were told they could leave the study at any time without losing their course credit. After the study, all participants were debriefed about the purpose of the research.

The rested group recalled an average of 18.4 words (SD = 4.1). The sleep-deprived group recalled an average of 12.7 words (SD = 4.6). This difference was statistically significant (p < .001), and the effect size was large (d = 1.31).

Participants who missed a night of sleep remembered about 6 fewer words than participants who slept. The researchers note that the sample included only college students and that future research should include other age groups.

a-social.title: Daily Social Media Use and Depressive Symptoms in Teens
a-social.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-social.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: Many people believe that social media use harms teens' mental health. Researchers examined whether the amount of time teens spend on social media is related to their depressive symptoms.
450 students from three public high schools in suburban Texas took part. Students were 14 to 18 years old (mean age 16.1). See the table for demographics.

Students completed a survey during class. Social media use was measured as the average number of minutes per day spent on social media apps over the past week, which students copied from the screen-time tool on their phones. Depressive symptoms were measured with the 20-item CES-D questionnaire, which gives a score from 0 to 60, with higher scores meaning more depressive symptoms. The researchers did not assign students to use social media for any amount of time. Parents gave written permission and students agreed to take part. Students did not write their names on the survey, so responses could not be traced back to them. Students were told they could skip any question or stop at any time.

Daily social media use was positively correlated with depressive symptoms (r = +.32, p < .01). Students who used social media for more than 3 hours a day had an average CES-D score of 21.4, while students who used it for less than 1 hour a day had an average score of 13.2.

Teens who spent more time on social media tended to report more depressive symptoms. The researchers caution that the study cannot show whether social media use causes depression, whether depressed teens use social media more, or whether another factor, such as poor sleep, affects both.

a-exercise.title: Aerobic Exercise and Symptoms of Generalized Anxiety Disorder
a-exercise.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-exercise.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) involves excessive, uncontrollable worry. Researchers tested the hypothesis that regular aerobic exercise reduces anxiety symptoms in adults with GAD.
84 adults diagnosed with GAD were recruited from mental health clinics in Toronto, Canada. Participants were 25 to 60 years old (mean age 41.3). See the table for demographics.

The study was approved by the university's research ethics board. A physician screened every participant to make sure exercise would be safe for them, and participants signed consent forms explaining the possible risks of exercise. Participants were then randomly assigned to one of two groups for 8 weeks. The aerobic group did 30 minutes of brisk walking or jogging three times a week, keeping their heart rate at 60–70% of its maximum. The control group did 30 minutes of light stretching three times a week. Anxiety was measured before and after the 8 weeks using the GAD-7 questionnaire, which gives a score from 0 to 21, with higher scores meaning more anxiety. At the end of the study, the control group was offered the aerobic exercise program.

The aerobic group's average GAD-7 score dropped from 13.8 to 7.9 (a decrease of 5.9 points). The stretching group's average score dropped from 13.5 to 11.7 (a decrease of 1.8 points). The difference between the groups was statistically significant (p = .004).

Adults with GAD who did aerobic exercise showed a much larger drop in anxiety symptoms than those who only stretched. The researchers note that most participants were women and that all were already receiving care at a clinic.

a-caffeine.title: Caffeine and Selective Attention on the Stroop Task
a-caffeine.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-caffeine.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: Selective attention is the ability to focus on one stimulus while ignoring others. Researchers tested the hypothesis that caffeine improves selective attention.

60 adults from a community in Seoul, South Korea, took part. All were 18 to 30 years old (mean age 23.4) and regularly drank 1 to 2 cups of coffee a day. People with heart conditions and pregnant women were not allowed to take part. See the table for demographics.

Participants were randomly assigned to drink a cup of coffee containing either 200 mg of caffeine or no caffeine (decaf). The two drinks looked and tasted the same, and neither the participants nor the researchers running the sessions knew who received which drink (double-blind). Thirty minutes later, participants completed a Stroop task with 60 color words printed in a different ink color (for example, the word RED printed in blue). Selective attention was measured as the average time in milliseconds participants took to correctly name the ink color. All participants gave informed consent and were told the study might involve caffeine. After the session, each participant was told which drink they had received and the full purpose of the study.

The caffeine group took an average of 712 milliseconds to name the ink color (SD = 88). The decaf group took an average of 784 milliseconds (SD = 95). The difference was statistically significant (p = .003).

Participants who had caffeine named ink colors about 72 milliseconds faster than those who had decaf. The researchers note that all participants were regular coffee drinkers and that the results may differ for people who do not usually consume caffeine.

a-cbt.title: Group Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Social Anxiety Disorder
a-cbt.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-cbt.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: Social anxiety disorder involves intense fear of being judged by others. Researchers tested the hypothesis that group cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) reduces social anxiety symptoms.
96 college students diagnosed with social anxiety disorder were recruited from two universities in California. Participants were 18 to 24 years old (mean age 20.2). See the table for demographics.

Participants were randomly assigned to group CBT or a waitlist control group. The CBT group attended 10 weekly 90-minute group sessions that used cognitive restructuring and gradual exposure using a fear hierarchy. The waitlist group received no treatment during the study and was offered the same CBT program after the study ended. Social anxiety was measured before and after the 10 weeks with the Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale (LSAS), scored from 0 to 144, with higher scores meaning more social anxiety. The clinicians who scored the LSAS did not know which group each participant was in. All participants gave informed consent. Data were stored using ID numbers instead of names, and participants were told they could leave the study at any time.

The CBT group's average LSAS score dropped from 78.2 to 49.6 (a decrease of 28.6 points). The waitlist group's average score dropped from 77.5 to 72.9 (a decrease of 4.6 points). The difference was statistically significant (p < .001) with a large effect size (d = 1.12). After treatment, 58% of the CBT group no longer met the criteria for social anxiety disorder, compared with 9% of the waitlist group.

Group CBT greatly reduced social anxiety symptoms in college students. The researchers note that all participants were college students and suggest testing the program with adults who are not in school.

a-hippo.title: Aerobic Exercise and Hippocampus Size in Older Adults
a-hippo.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-hippo.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: The hippocampus helps store new long-term memories and shrinks with age. Researchers tested the hypothesis that aerobic exercise increases hippocampus size in older adults.
120 adults aged 60 to 80 (mean age 67.4) living in a small city in Illinois took part. None had dementia. See the table for demographics.

Participants were randomly assigned to a walking group or a stretching group for one year. The walking group walked briskly for 40 minutes, three days a week. The stretching group did 40 minutes of stretching and toning, three days a week. Hippocampus size was measured as the volume of the hippocampus in cubic centimeters on an MRI scan taken before and after the year. The study was approved by the university's review board, and every participant was cleared by their doctor before starting.

The walking group's hippocampus volume increased by 2.1% on average. The stretching group's hippocampus volume decreased by 1.4% on average. The difference between groups was statistically significant (p < .01).
Walking reversed about one to two years of age-related shrinkage. The researchers note that all participants were healthy enough to exercise and lived in one city.

a-games.title: Action Video Games and Reaction Time
a-games.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-games.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: Some people believe that action video games make players react faster. Researchers examined whether hours of action video game play are related to reaction time.
200 students from a community college in Arizona took part. Participants were 18 to 26 years old (mean age 20.8). See the table for demographics.

Participants reported how many hours per week they spent playing action video games over the past month. Reaction time was measured as the average number of milliseconds it took participants to press a key after a dot appeared on a screen, over 50 trials. The researchers did not ask anyone to play video games. Participants signed consent forms, and their data were stored under ID numbers instead of names.

Hours of action video game play were negatively correlated with reaction time (r = -.41, p < .001). Players who gamed more than 10 hours a week averaged 285 ms, while those who did not play averaged 342 ms.
More gaming was associated with faster reaction times. The researchers note that people who already have fast reactions might be drawn to action games.

a-music.title: Background Music and Reading Comprehension
a-music.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-music.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: Many students listen to music while they study. Researchers tested the hypothesis that music with lyrics hurts reading comprehension.
90 students from one high school in Georgia took part. Students were 15 to 17 years old (mean age 16.0). See the table for demographics.

Students were randomly assigned to read a 1,200-word passage while listening to popular music with lyrics, the same music without lyrics, or silence. Reading comprehension was measured as the number of correct answers on a 20-question multiple-choice test taken right after reading. Parents signed permission forms and students agreed to take part. Students were told they could stop at any time without it affecting their grades.

The silence group averaged 15.6 correct answers. The instrumental group averaged 14.9. The lyrics group averaged 11.8. The lyrics group scored significantly lower than both other groups (p < .01), while the silence and instrumental groups did not differ significantly.
Lyrics, not music itself, appeared to interfere with reading. The researchers suggest that processing words in songs competes with processing words on the page.

a-notes.title: Laptop vs. Handwritten Notes and Conceptual Learning
a-notes.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-notes.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: Researchers tested the hypothesis that taking notes by hand leads to better understanding of lecture material than typing notes on a laptop.
146 undergraduates at a university in New Jersey took part for course credit. Participants were 18 to 23 years old (mean age 19.8). See the table for demographics.

Participants were randomly assigned to take notes either by hand or on a laptop while watching a 15-minute recorded lecture. One week later, they took a test. Conceptual learning was measured as the number of points (out of 10) earned on five short-answer questions that asked participants to apply ideas from the lecture. Participants gave informed consent, and after the test they were told the full purpose of the study.

Handwriting participants scored an average of 6.8 points on conceptual questions. Laptop participants scored an average of 5.1 points (p = .002). Laptop users wrote 62% more words, often copying the lecture word for word.
Typing seemed to encourage copying without processing. The researchers note that all participants were students at one university.

a-bedscreen.title: Screen Time Before Bed and Sleep Onset
a-bedscreen.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-bedscreen.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: Researchers examined whether using phones and tablets before bed is related to how long it takes teens to fall asleep.
310 middle school students from two schools in Oregon took part. Students were 11 to 14 years old (mean age 12.6). See the table for demographics.

For two weeks, students wore a wrist sleep tracker and kept a diary. Bedtime screen use was measured as the number of minutes of screen use recorded in the hour before lights out. Sleep onset was measured as the number of minutes between lights out and falling asleep, as recorded by the wrist tracker. The researchers did not tell students how to use their devices. Parents gave consent and students gave assent. Names were replaced with codes before data were analyzed.

Bedtime screen use was positively correlated with time to fall asleep (r = +.38, p < .001). Students with more than 45 minutes of bedtime screen use took an average of 31 minutes to fall asleep, compared with 14 minutes for students with no screen use.
More screen time before bed was associated with taking longer to fall asleep. The researchers point out that anxious students might both use screens more and have trouble sleeping.

a-bluelight.title: Blue-Light-Blocking Glasses and Sleep Quality
a-bluelight.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-bluelight.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: Light from screens can interfere with circadian rhythms. Researchers tested the hypothesis that wearing blue-light-blocking glasses in the evening improves sleep.
48 adults with insomnia symptoms from a city in Norway took part. Participants were 22 to 55 years old (mean age 38.5). See the table for demographics.

Participants were randomly assigned to wear amber blue-light-blocking glasses or clear placebo glasses for the 3 hours before bed for two weeks. Participants did not know which glasses blocked blue light. Sleep quality was measured as the score on the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), a questionnaire scored 0 to 21, where lower scores mean better sleep. The study was approved by a regional ethics committee, and participants signed consent forms.

The amber-glasses group's PSQI scores improved from 11.2 to 7.4 (a drop of 3.8 points). The placebo group's scores improved from 11.0 to 10.1 (a drop of 0.9 points). The difference was statistically significant (p = .01).
Blocking blue light in the evening improved sleep quality more than wearing clear glasses. The researchers note that the sample was small and all from one country.

a-naps.title: Afternoon Naps and Memory Consolidation
a-naps.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-naps.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: Researchers tested the hypothesis that a short afternoon nap helps people hold on to newly learned information.
64 university students in Germany took part. Participants were 19 to 28 years old (mean age 22.9). See the table for demographics.

All participants learned 50 pairs of words at noon. They were then randomly assigned to take a 60-minute nap in the lab or to watch a nature video for 60 minutes while staying awake. At 5 p.m., memory was measured as the percentage of word pairs participants correctly recalled when shown the first word of each pair. Participants gave informed consent and were told they could leave at any time.
The nap group recalled 78% of word pairs on average. The video group recalled 63% (p < .001).
A short nap helped participants retain new information. The researchers note that all participants were university students in one country.

a-gratitude.title: Gratitude Journaling and Depressive Symptoms
a-gratitude.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-gratitude.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: Researchers tested the hypothesis that writing about things you are grateful for reduces depressive symptoms.
150 adults recruited online from across the United States took part. Participants were 21 to 64 years old (mean age 37.2). See the table for demographics.

Participants were randomly assigned to write three things they were grateful for each night or to write three things that happened that day, for 4 weeks. Depressive symptoms were measured with the PHQ-9 questionnaire (scored 0 to 27; higher = more symptoms) before and after the 4 weeks. Participants agreed to an online consent form. People with severe depression scores at the start were referred to mental health services instead of being included.

The gratitude group's PHQ-9 scores dropped from 10.4 to 7.1 (a drop of 3.3 points). The daily-events group's scores dropped from 10.1 to 9.4 (a drop of 0.7 points). The difference was statistically significant (p = .02), with a small-to-medium effect size (d = 0.38).
Gratitude journaling produced a modest drop in depressive symptoms. The researchers note that participants volunteered online and were mostly women.

a-cold.title: Perceived Stress and Catching a Cold
a-cold.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-cold.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: Researchers tested the hypothesis that people under more stress are more likely to get sick when exposed to a cold virus.
276 healthy adults from Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, took part and were paid. Participants were 18 to 55 years old (mean age 30.1). See the table for demographics.

Participants first completed the Perceived Stress Scale (scored 0 to 40). Researchers then split them into a high-stress group (top third of scores) and a low-stress group (bottom third). All participants were given nasal drops containing a mild cold virus and stayed in a hotel for 5 days. Getting a cold was defined as having both the virus in nasal samples and clinical symptoms such as congestion, as judged by a doctor who did not know participants' stress scores. The study was approved by the university's review board, and participants were monitored by doctors throughout.
47% of the high-stress group developed a cold, compared with 27% of the low-stress group (p < .01).
People reporting more stress were more likely to get sick. Because stress was measured, not assigned, the researchers caution that other differences between the groups might matter.

a-aces.title: Adverse Childhood Experiences and Adult Heart Disease
a-aces.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-aces.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) include abuse, neglect, and household dysfunction. Researchers examined whether the number of ACEs a person had is related to heart disease in adulthood.
8,400 adults who visited a health clinic in California completed the survey. Participants were 25 to 85 years old (mean age 56). See the table for demographics.

Participants filled out a confidential questionnaire counting how many of 10 types of ACEs they experienced before age 18 (scores 0 to 10). Heart disease was measured from each participant's medical record as whether a doctor had ever diagnosed coronary heart disease. Nobody was assigned to any condition. Participants consented to their medical records being used, and records were stored without names.
People with 4 or more ACEs were 2.2 times as likely to have heart disease as people with 0 ACEs. The number of ACEs was positively correlated with heart disease (r = +.21, p < .001).
More childhood adversity was linked to a higher risk of heart disease decades later. The researchers note that participants all had health insurance through one provider.

a-meditate.title: Meditation App Use and Cortisol
a-meditate.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-meditate.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: Cortisol is a stress hormone. Researchers tested the hypothesis that a daily meditation app lowers stress hormone levels in nurses.
82 hospital nurses in Chicago, Illinois, took part. Participants were 24 to 59 years old (mean age 39.7). See the table for demographics.

Nurses were randomly assigned to use a meditation app for 10 minutes a day for 6 weeks or to a waitlist control group that got the app after the study. Stress was measured as the level of cortisol in saliva samples collected at 8 a.m. on the same day each week. The hospital's ethics board approved the study, and nurses were told that taking part would not affect their jobs. Data were labeled with ID numbers.
The app group's average morning cortisol fell by 18%. The waitlist group's fell by 3% (p = .01).
Brief daily meditation lowered a biological measure of stress. The researchers note the sample was mostly women from one hospital.

a-placebo.title: Expectations and Pain: A Placebo Cream Study
a-placebo.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-placebo.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: Researchers tested the hypothesis that simply believing you received a painkiller reduces the pain you feel.
60 university students in Ontario, Canada, took part. Participants were 18 to 25 years old (mean age 20.5). See the table for demographics.

All participants had a mild heat stimulus applied to their forearm. Before the heat, participants were randomly assigned to have a cream described as "a powerful pain reliever" or the same cream described as "a moisturizer." The cream had no active ingredient in either case. Pain was measured as each participant's rating of the heat on a 0 to 10 scale. The heat was kept below the level that could damage skin, and participants could stop the heat at any time. Afterward, everyone was told the cream was inactive and why deception was needed.
The "pain reliever" group rated the heat at 4.1 on average. The "moisturizer" group rated it at 6.3 (p < .001).
Expecting pain relief reduced pain ratings even though the cream was inactive.

a-cafeteria.title: Phones at the Lunch Table: A Naturalistic Observation
a-cafeteria.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-cafeteria.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: Researchers wanted to describe how phone use relates to face-to-face conversation among teens in a natural setting.
Researchers observed 240 students during lunch at four public high schools in Ohio. Based on school records, students were 14 to 18 years old. See the table for school demographics.

Two trained observers sat in each cafeteria and recorded behavior without interacting with students. Every 2 minutes, observers recorded whether each student at a table was looking at a phone and whether they were talking with someone at the table. Conversation was measured as the percentage of 2-minute checks in which a student was talking with someone at the table. Observers did not record names or any identifying information, and the schools approved the study.
Students who had a phone out on the table were talking during 41% of checks, compared with 68% for students without a phone out. The two observers agreed on 94% of their recordings.
Visible phones were associated with less face-to-face conversation. The researchers note that they could not tell why students had their phones out.

a-casehm.title: A Case Study of Memory After Hippocampus Damage
a-casehm.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-casehm.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: Researchers studied a rare case to learn which brain areas are needed to form new memories.
The study focused on one 52-year-old man, referred to as "Patient R.K.," from Boston, Massachusetts. A viral infection had damaged both of his hippocampi. Before the illness he worked as an engineer.

Over 3 years, researchers conducted in-depth interviews, brain scans, and memory tests with R.K. New memory formation was measured as the number of 15 objects R.K. could name 30 minutes after seeing them. R.K. and his wife gave written consent, his name and identifying details were changed in all reports, and he could stop any session when he was tired.

R.K. recalled an average of 1 out of 15 objects after 30 minutes, compared with an average of 11 out of 15 for healthy men his age. He could still remember events from before his illness and could learn new motor skills, such as tracing a star in a mirror, even though he did not remember practicing.
The hippocampus appears necessary for forming new long-term memories of facts and events but not for older memories or motor skills.

a-casesplit.title: A Case Study of a Split-Brain Patient
a-casesplit.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-casesplit.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: Researchers studied a patient whose corpus callosum had been cut to stop severe seizures, to learn how the two hemispheres share information.
The study focused on one 34-year-old woman, called "Patient V.J.," from Ohio, who is right-handed and had the surgery at age 27.

Over 2 years, researchers ran 40 testing sessions. In each test, a word flashed briefly to either her left or right visual field. Language ability for each hemisphere was measured as the percentage of trials in which she could correctly say the word out loud. V.J. signed a consent form explaining all procedures, could take breaks or stop any session, and her identity was kept confidential.

V.J. correctly said 96% of words flashed to her right visual field but only 4% of words flashed to her left visual field. However, she could point to the correct object with her left hand on 89% of left-visual-field trials.
Information reaching only the right hemisphere could guide her left hand but could not be put into words.

a-metassri.title: A Meta-Analysis of Antidepressants for Depression
a-metassri.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-metassri.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: Researchers wanted to know how well SSRI antidepressants work compared with a placebo.

The researchers combined data from 52 published studies that included a total of 13,400 adults diagnosed with major depressive disorder. Studies were from 18 countries. See the table for the combined sample.

The researchers searched research databases for randomized studies comparing an SSRI with a placebo pill for at least 6 weeks. Improvement was measured as the percentage of patients in each study whose depression scores dropped by at least half (called "response"). All included studies had been approved by ethics boards and had informed consent from participants.

Across all studies, 54% of patients taking SSRIs responded, compared with 38% of patients taking a placebo. The overall effect size was small to medium (d = 0.31). SSRIs worked better for people with severe depression than for people with mild depression.
SSRIs were more effective than placebo, but placebos also helped many patients.

a-metaex.title: A Meta-Analysis of Exercise and Depression
a-metaex.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-metaex.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: Researchers asked whether exercise reduces depressive symptoms, combining evidence from many studies.
The researchers combined 35 randomized studies that included 2,500 adults with depression from 14 countries. See the table for the combined sample.

Studies were included if they randomly assigned adults with depression to an exercise program or a no-exercise control for at least 4 weeks. Depressive symptoms were measured in each study with standard questionnaires, and the researchers combined the results as an overall effect size. All included studies reported ethics approval.

Across studies, exercise reduced depressive symptoms with a moderate overall effect size (d = 0.56). The effect was larger for programs with 3 or more sessions a week (d = 0.69) than for programs with fewer sessions (d = 0.38).
Exercise was an effective way to reduce depressive symptoms, and more frequent programs worked better.

a-mindset.title: Growth Mindset Lessons and Math Grades
a-mindset.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-mindset.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: A growth mindset is the belief that abilities can improve with effort. Researchers tested the hypothesis that a short growth mindset program raises math grades.
1,200 ninth graders from 10 public high schools in North Carolina took part. Students were 14 to 15 years old. See the table for demographics.

Students were randomly assigned to complete two 25-minute online lessons about how the brain grows with effort (growth mindset) or two 25-minute lessons about brain functions (control). Math achievement was measured as each student's end-of-year math grade point average on a 4.0 scale. Parents were notified and could opt their child out, and students' records were analyzed without names.
Growth mindset students finished the year with an average math GPA of 2.48; control students averaged 2.39 (p = .03). The effect size was small (d = 0.10).
The program produced a small but statistically significant improvement in math grades.

a-phonedesk.title: Phone Presence and Working Memory
a-phonedesk.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-phonedesk.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: Researchers tested the hypothesis that simply having your phone nearby reduces the mental capacity available for other tasks.
520 undergraduate students at a university in Texas took part. Participants were 18 to 24 years old (mean age 20.1). See the table for demographics.

Participants were randomly assigned to leave their phone (silenced) face down on the desk, in their bag, or in another room. They then completed a working memory task. Working memory was measured as the number of letters (out of 75) participants correctly remembered while solving math problems. Participants gave informed consent and were debriefed about the purpose after the session.
The phone-on-desk group remembered an average of 30.9 letters. The bag group averaged 31.6. The other-room group averaged 33.6 (p = .03 for desk vs. other room).
The closer the phone, the lower the working memory performance, even though phones were silent.

a-gorilla.title: Task Difficulty and Inattentional Blindness
a-gorilla.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-gorilla.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: Inattentional blindness is failing to notice a visible object when attention is directed elsewhere. Researchers tested the hypothesis that a harder task increases inattentional blindness.
120 adults at a science museum in Illinois volunteered. Participants were 18 to 70 years old (mean age 34.8). See the table for demographics.

Participants watched a 75-second video of people passing basketballs. They were randomly assigned to an easy task (count total passes) or a hard task (count bounce passes and aerial passes separately). Halfway through, a person in a gorilla costume walked through the scene. Noticing was measured as whether participants answered "yes" when asked afterward if they saw anything unusual and could describe the gorilla. Participants agreed to take part and were told afterward about the gorilla and the study's purpose.
72% of the easy-task group noticed the gorilla. Only 45% of the hard-task group noticed it (p = .003).
When attention was more heavily focused, more people missed an obvious, unexpected object.

a-hearing.title: Age and Hearing Thresholds
a-hearing.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-hearing.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: The absolute threshold is the weakest stimulus a person can detect 50% of the time. Researchers examined whether age is related to the absolute threshold for high-pitched sounds.
400 adults from Melbourne, Australia, took part. Participants were 20 to 79 years old (mean age 49.5). See the table for demographics.

Each participant sat in a soundproof booth and heard high-pitched (8,000 Hz) tones at different volumes. Hearing threshold was measured as the quietest volume, in decibels, that a participant detected on 50% of trials. Age was taken from each participant's birth date. No one was assigned to groups. Participants signed consent forms and anyone with a threshold suggesting hearing loss was given a referral to an audiologist.

Age was positively correlated with hearing threshold (r = +.67, p < .001). Participants in their 20s had an average threshold of 12 decibels, while participants in their 70s had an average of 54 decibels.
Older adults needed much louder high-pitched sounds to detect them.

a-vr.title: Virtual Reality Distraction and Pain During Dental Work
a-vr.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-vr.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: Gate control theory says distraction can "close the gate" to pain signals. Researchers tested the hypothesis that virtual reality distraction reduces pain during dental cleanings.
80 dental patients at a clinic in Spain took part. Participants were 18 to 65 years old (mean age 41.0). See the table for demographics.

Patients were randomly assigned to wear a VR headset showing an underwater world during their cleaning or to have a standard cleaning with no headset. Pain was measured as the patient's rating on a 0 to 100 scale right after the cleaning. Patients signed consent forms and were told they could remove the headset or stop the cleaning at any time.
The VR group rated their pain at 22 on average. The standard group rated it at 41 (p < .001).
Immersive distraction cut pain ratings nearly in half.

a-supertaste.title: Taste Sensitivity and Vegetable Eating
a-supertaste.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-supertaste.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: Supertasters have more taste buds and experience bitter tastes more strongly. Researchers examined whether taste sensitivity is related to how many vegetables people eat.
250 adults from Vermont took part. Participants were 20 to 65 years old (mean age 44.2). See the table for demographics.

Taste sensitivity was measured as the number of taste buds counted in a 6 mm circle on the tip of the tongue, using blue dye and a magnified photo. Vegetable intake was measured as the number of vegetable servings per week reported in a food diary kept for 2 weeks. Participants were not assigned to eat anything. Participants gave informed consent and were told they could withdraw at any time.

The number of taste buds was negatively correlated with vegetable servings per week (r = -.29, p < .01). People with the most taste buds ate 11 servings a week on average, compared with 17 servings for people with the fewest.
People with more taste buds tended to eat fewer vegetables, possibly because many vegetables taste bitter to them.

a-erp.title: Exposure and Response Prevention for OCD
a-erp.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-erp.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: Exposure and response prevention (ERP) has people face triggers without doing their compulsions. Researchers tested the hypothesis that ERP reduces OCD symptoms more than relaxation training.
72 adults diagnosed with OCD from two clinics in Massachusetts took part. Participants were 19 to 58 years old (mean age 33.6). See the table for demographics.

Participants were randomly assigned to 12 weekly sessions of ERP or 12 weekly sessions of relaxation training. OCD symptoms were measured with the Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS), scored 0 to 40, by an interviewer who did not know each participant's group. The hospital review board approved the study, participants signed consent forms, and relaxation participants were offered ERP afterward.
ERP participants' Y-BOCS scores dropped from 26.1 to 14.3 (11.8 points). Relaxation participants' scores dropped from 25.7 to 22.9 (2.8 points). The difference was significant (p < .001).
ERP greatly reduced OCD symptoms compared with relaxation alone.

a-dogs.title: Service Dogs and PTSD Symptoms in Veterans
a-dogs.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-dogs.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: Researchers tested the hypothesis that having a trained service dog reduces PTSD symptoms in military veterans.
140 military veterans diagnosed with PTSD from VA clinics in three states took part. Participants were 25 to 68 years old (mean age 44.9). See the table for demographics.

Veterans were randomly assigned to receive a service dog right away or to a waitlist group that continued usual care and received a dog after 3 months. PTSD symptoms were measured with the PCL-5 checklist (scored 0 to 80, higher = more severe). Veterans gave informed consent, could leave the study at any time while keeping their usual care, and their information was kept confidential.
After 3 months, the service dog group's PCL-5 scores dropped by 12.4 points on average. The waitlist group's scores dropped by 4.1 points (p = .002).
Service dogs led to a meaningful drop in PTSD symptoms on top of usual care.

a-thinideal.title: Thin-Ideal Images and Body Dissatisfaction
a-thinideal.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-thinideal.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: Researchers tested the hypothesis that looking at idealized thin images on social media increases body dissatisfaction in young women.
160 female college students in Sydney, Australia, took part. Participants were 17 to 25 years old (mean age 19.4). See the table for demographics.

Participants were randomly assigned to scroll through 30 social media posts showing thin, edited models or 30 posts showing travel destinations, for 10 minutes. Body dissatisfaction was measured as the rating on a 0 to 100 line ("How dissatisfied are you with your body right now?") before and after scrolling. Participants were screened for eating disorders, and anyone at risk was not included and was given support resources. Everyone was debriefed and shown an article on how photos are edited.
Body dissatisfaction increased by 14.2 points in the thin-image group and by 1.3 points in the travel group (p < .001).
Just 10 minutes of thin-ideal images raised body dissatisfaction.

a-adhdbreaks.title: Movement Breaks and On-Task Behavior in Students with ADHD
a-adhdbreaks.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-adhdbreaks.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: Researchers tested the hypothesis that short movement breaks help students with ADHD stay on task.
54 students diagnosed with ADHD from six elementary schools in Florida took part. Students were 7 to 11 years old (mean age 9.1). See the table for demographics.

Students were randomly assigned to have three 5-minute movement breaks (jumping, stretching) during the school day or three 5-minute quiet reading breaks. On-task behavior was measured as the percentage of 15-second intervals in which a trained observer, who did not know each student's group, saw the student looking at their work or the teacher during a 30-minute math lesson. Parents gave written consent, students agreed, and their names were not used in reports.
Students with movement breaks were on task during 79% of intervals. Students with reading breaks were on task during 62% (p = .004).
Short bursts of physical activity improved focus during class.

a-cannabis.title: Teen Cannabis Use and Later Psychosis
a-cannabis.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-cannabis.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: Researchers examined whether heavy cannabis use in the teen years is related to developing a psychotic disorder in adulthood.
45,000 men who were drafted into the military in Sweden at age 18 were followed for 15 years. See the table for demographics.

At age 18, each man reported how many times he had used cannabis. Psychosis was measured as whether he was later diagnosed with schizophrenia or another psychotic disorder in national hospital records. The researchers did not assign anyone to use cannabis. The national ethics board approved the study, and records were linked using codes rather than names.

Men who had used cannabis more than 50 times by age 18 were 3.1 times as likely to be diagnosed with a psychotic disorder as men who never used it. Use was positively correlated with later diagnosis (r = +.12, p < .001).
Heavy teen cannabis use was linked to later psychosis. Because the study was correlational, the researchers note that early symptoms might have led some men to use cannabis.

a-lithium.title: Lithium and Relapse in Bipolar Disorder
a-lithium.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-lithium.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: Mood stabilizers such as lithium are used to treat bipolar disorder. Researchers tested the hypothesis that lithium prevents mood episodes better than a placebo.
180 adults with bipolar I disorder from hospitals in the United Kingdom took part. Participants were 21 to 65 years old (mean age 42.0). See the table for demographics.

All participants were currently stable. They were randomly assigned to take lithium or an identical placebo pill daily for 18 months, in a double-blind design. Relapse was measured as having a manic or depressive episode severe enough to need a change in treatment, as decided by a psychiatrist. Participants gave informed consent, their blood was checked monthly for safe lithium levels, and anyone who relapsed was immediately given full treatment.
By 18 months, 31% of the lithium group had relapsed, compared with 63% of the placebo group (p < .001).
Lithium cut the relapse rate roughly in half.

a-tms.title: rTMS for Treatment-Resistant Depression
a-tms.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-tms.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) uses magnetic pulses to stimulate the brain. Researchers tested the hypothesis that rTMS reduces depression in people who did not improve with medication.
120 adults with treatment-resistant depression from four clinics in South Korea took part. Participants were 20 to 64 years old (mean age 45.3). See the table for demographics.

Participants were randomly assigned to real rTMS or "sham" rTMS, which looked and sounded the same but did not deliver magnetic pulses. Both groups had 20 sessions over 4 weeks. Depression was measured with the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAM-D, 0 to 52) by raters who did not know the group. Participants gave informed consent and were told they might receive the sham treatment; sham participants were offered real rTMS afterward.

The real rTMS group's HAM-D scores dropped by 9.6 points on average. The sham group's scores dropped by 4.2 points (p = .001). 38% of the real group went into remission, compared with 15% of the sham group.
rTMS reduced depression in patients who had not responded to medication, with no memory side effects reported.

a-lighttx.title: Bright Light Therapy and Seasonal Depression
a-lighttx.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-lighttx.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: Researchers tested the hypothesis that daily bright light therapy reduces depression that appears in winter.
56 adults with winter-pattern depression from Minnesota took part. Participants were 22 to 60 years old (mean age 39.8). See the table for demographics.

Participants were randomly assigned to sit in front of a bright light box (10,000 lux) or a dim red light (placebo) for 30 minutes each morning for 6 weeks. Depression was measured with the Beck Depression Inventory (BDI, 0 to 63). The study was approved by the university's review board, participants signed consent forms, and those who got worse were referred for additional treatment.
The bright light group's BDI scores dropped from 24.5 to 11.9. The dim light group's scores dropped from 23.8 to 19.6 (p < .001).
Bright morning light substantially reduced winter depression symptoms.

a-selfies.title: Narcissism and Selfie Posting
a-selfies.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-selfies.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: Researchers examined whether narcissistic traits are related to how often people post selfies.
800 adults in the United Kingdom completed the study online. Participants were 18 to 40 years old (mean age 27.3). See the table for demographics.

Narcissism was measured as the score on the 16-item Narcissistic Personality Inventory (NPI-16, 0 to 16). Selfie posting was measured as the number of selfies each participant posted on social media in the past month, counted from their own accounts. No one was assigned to post anything. Participants agreed to an online consent form, and responses were anonymous.

Narcissism scores were positively correlated with selfie posting (r = +.28, p < .001). Participants in the top 10% of narcissism scores posted an average of 19 selfies a month, compared with 6 for the bottom 10%.
People with more narcissistic traits tended to post more selfies. The study could not tell whether posting selfies increases narcissism or the other way around.

a-cbti.title: CBT for Insomnia vs. Sleep Hygiene Advice
a-cbti.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-cbti.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: Researchers tested the hypothesis that cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) improves sleep more than basic sleep hygiene advice.
110 adults with insomnia from a sleep clinic in Montreal, Canada, took part. Participants were 25 to 70 years old (mean age 51.2). See the table for demographics.

Participants were randomly assigned to 6 weekly sessions of CBT-I (changing beliefs about sleep and setting a strict sleep schedule) or a single session of sleep hygiene advice (avoid caffeine, keep the room dark). Insomnia was measured as the number of minutes participants were awake after first falling asleep, averaged from 2 weeks of sleep diaries. Participants gave informed consent, and the hygiene group was offered CBT-I after the study.
Minutes awake per night dropped from 72 to 31 in the CBT-I group and from 70 to 61 in the sleep hygiene group (p < .001).
CBT-I greatly reduced nighttime waking compared with basic advice.

a-alcoholdrive.title: Alcohol and Driving Errors in a Simulator
a-alcoholdrive.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-alcoholdrive.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: Alcohol is a depressant. Researchers tested the hypothesis that a moderate dose of alcohol increases driving errors.
40 adults from Wellington, New Zealand, took part. All were 21 to 35 years old (mean age 26.7), held a driver's license, and were moderate drinkers. See the table for demographics.

Participants were randomly assigned to drink orange juice mixed with alcohol (bringing them to a blood alcohol level of about 0.06%) or orange juice with a small amount of alcohol rubbed on the rim of the glass for smell (placebo). After 30 minutes, they drove a 20-minute route in a driving simulator. Driving errors were measured as the number of times the simulated car crossed a lane line. Participants were screened by a doctor, stayed in the lab until their blood alcohol was zero, and were driven home by taxi.
The alcohol group crossed lane lines 14.3 times on average. The placebo group crossed lane lines 6.1 times (p < .001).
Even moderate alcohol more than doubled lane errors.

a-energy.title: Energy Drinks and Teen Sleep
a-energy.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-energy.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: Researchers examined whether drinking energy drinks is related to how much sleep teens get.
1,500 high school students in Minnesota completed a statewide school survey. Students were 14 to 18 years old (mean age 15.9). See the table for demographics.

Energy drink use was measured as the number of energy drinks students reported drinking in the past 7 days. Sleep was measured as the number of hours students reported sleeping on a typical school night. Students were not assigned to drink anything. The survey was anonymous, parents could opt their child out, and students could skip any question.

Energy drink use was negatively correlated with school-night sleep (r = -.26, p < .001). Students who had 5 or more energy drinks a week slept 6.1 hours a night on average, compared with 7.3 hours for students who had none.
Teens who drank more energy drinks slept less. The researchers note that teens who sleep less might drink energy drinks to stay awake.

a-hindsight.title: Hindsight Bias After an Election
a-hindsight.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-hindsight.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: Hindsight bias is believing, after learning an outcome, that you would have predicted it. Researchers tested the hypothesis that learning an outcome makes people think it was more predictable.
200 adults from across Canada were recruited online. Participants were 18 to 74 years old (mean age 41.6). See the table for demographics.

All participants read the same description of a close election between two candidates. They were randomly assigned to be told that Candidate A won, that Candidate B won, or not told the result. Hindsight bias was measured as how likely participants said the winner was to win, rated from 0% to 100%, as if they had predicted it before the election. Participants gave consent, were told the election was fictional at the end, and their responses were anonymous.
Participants told that a candidate won rated that candidate's chance of winning at 71% on average. Participants not told the result rated each candidate at about 50% (p < .001).
Learning the outcome made the result seem much more predictable than it really was.

a-framing.title: Wording Effects in a Health Survey
a-framing.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-framing.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: Researchers tested the hypothesis that the way a question is worded changes how people answer it.
300 adults at a shopping mall in Atlanta, Georgia, took part. Participants were 18 to 80 years old (mean age 43.5). See the table for demographics.

Participants read about a new surgery and were randomly assigned to one of two versions: "90% of patients survive" or "10% of patients die." Support was measured as the percentage of participants who answered "yes" to "Would you choose this surgery?" The facts were the same in both versions. Participants agreed verbally, no names were collected, and they were told about the two versions afterward.
72% of people who read "90% survive" said yes. Only 44% of people who read "10% die" said yes (p < .001).
Equal information framed in different words led to very different choices.

a-cheating.title: Anonymity and Honest Answers About Cheating
a-cheating.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-cheating.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: Social desirability bias is giving answers that make you look good. Researchers tested the hypothesis that students report more cheating when their answers are anonymous.
400 students from two public high schools in Michigan took part. Students were 14 to 18 years old (mean age 16.2). See the table for demographics.

Students were randomly assigned to answer a survey either face to face with a teacher writing down their answers or on an anonymous paper form dropped into a sealed box. Reported cheating was measured as the percentage of students who answered "yes" to "Have you cheated on a test this school year?" Parents could opt their child out, students could skip questions, and no student was punished for any answer.
58% of students in the anonymous group said they had cheated, compared with 21% in the face-to-face group (p < .001).
Students were nearly three times as likely to admit cheating when anonymous.

a-hassles.title: Daily Hassles and Mood in College Students
a-hassles.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-hassles.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: Daily hassles are small everyday stressors. Researchers examined whether the number of daily hassles students experience is related to their mood.
150 students at a university in Colorado took part. Participants were 18 to 24 years old (mean age 20.4). See the table for demographics.

For 14 days, students received a phone survey every evening. Daily hassles were measured as the number of items students checked on a list of 20 hassles (such as "running late," "phone died," "argument with roommate"). Mood was measured as their rating of their mood that day from 1 (very bad) to 10 (very good). Students were not assigned to experience hassles. They gave informed consent and their answers were stored using ID numbers.
The number of daily hassles was negatively correlated with mood (r = -.44, p < .001). On days with 5 or more hassles, the average mood rating was 4.8, compared with 7.6 on days with 0 or 1 hassle.
More daily hassles were linked to worse daily mood.

a-groupdep.title: Group vs. Individual Therapy for Depression
a-groupdep.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-groupdep.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: Researchers tested the hypothesis that group therapy is as effective as individual therapy for depression.
160 adults with major depressive disorder from community clinics in Ontario, Canada, took part. Participants were 20 to 65 years old (mean age 40.7). See the table for demographics.

Participants were randomly assigned to 12 weeks of individual CBT (one therapist, one client) or group CBT (one therapist, 8 clients). Both used the same lessons. Depression was measured with the PHQ-9 (0 to 27). Cost was measured as the clinic's total therapist cost per client. Participants gave informed consent, group members agreed to keep what others shared private, and anyone at risk of self-harm received immediate individual care.

PHQ-9 scores dropped by 7.8 points in the individual group and 7.2 points in the group-therapy group. The difference was not statistically significant (p = .48). Group therapy cost $420 per client, compared with $1,560 for individual therapy.
Group therapy reduced depression about as well as individual therapy at a much lower cost.

a-reappraise.title: Rethinking Stress Before a Test
a-reappraise.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-reappraise.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: Researchers tested the hypothesis that learning to view stress as helpful (eustress) improves test performance.
90 students preparing for a graduate admissions exam at a university in Massachusetts took part. Participants were 21 to 30 years old (mean age 23.8). See the table for demographics.

Before a practice exam, participants were randomly assigned to read a short message saying that feeling anxious can improve performance by sending more energy to the brain, or a message with general test-taking tips. Students with dog allergies or fear of dogs were not included, all gave consent, and handlers kept the dogs on leashes.

Over one year, researchers interviewed E.M. in depth and tested her repeatedly. Consistency was measured as the percentage of numbers 0 to 9 for which E.M. chose the same color on a 100-color chart when tested one year apart, without warning. E.M. gave informed consent, could stop testing whenever she wanted, and her identity was kept confidential. Researchers compared her with 20 non-synesthetes who were asked to invent and remember number-color pairs.
E.M. chose the same color for 100% of numbers after one year. The comparison group matched only 31% of their colors after just one week.
E.M.'s number-color pairs were highly consistent and automatic, supporting the idea that synesthesia is a real perceptual experience.

Over 6 weeks, trained observers stood at the edge of the playground and did not interact with children. Aggression was measured as the number of hitting, pushing, or kicking acts per child during a 30-minute recess. Observers recorded during days with free play and days when teachers organized games. Schools gave permission, no names were recorded, and observers stopped any fight that could cause injury.
Children committed 1.8 aggressive acts per recess on free-play days and 0.7 acts on organized-game days. Two observers agreed on 91% of recorded acts.

Identical twins' anxiety scores were correlated at r = +.52. Fraternal twins' scores were correlated at r = +.24 (p < .001 for the difference).

Withdrawal was measured as the number of hours with a headache, recorded in a diary over the 2 days. Binocular vision made distance judgments much more accurate, especially for nearby objects.

Evidence: Students who limited their social media use to 30 minutes per day showed significant reductions in loneliness and depression compared to the control group (Source 1).
Explanation: This supports the claim that adolescents should reduce social media use, because spending less time on these platforms decreased negative psychological outcomes.
Application: This can be explained through social comparison theory: when adolescents spend less time viewing curated posts from peers, they engage in fewer upward social comparisons, which reduces feelings of inadequacy and depressive symptoms.
