e-socialmedia.title: Develop and justify an argument about whether adolescents should limit their social media use.
e-socialmedia.label: Practice sources from Phineas's AP Psych kit, summarized and simplified.

blocks.p: 143 undergraduates (ages 18–22) at a university in Pennsylvania were randomly assigned to limit social media to 30 minutes per day or to use it as usual for 3 weeks. Students who limited their use showed significant reductions in loneliness and depression compared with the control group (p < .05). Those who started with higher depression scores improved the most.

blocks.h: Source 2: Screen Time and Teen Depression
blocks.p: A survey of 6,595 U.S. teens ages 12–15 found that teens who spent more than 3 hours a day on social media were twice as likely to report high levels of anxiety and depression symptoms as teens who did not use social media. The relationship remained after accounting for gender and family income. The study was correlational.

In a study of 1,200 adolescents ages 13–17 in the United Kingdom, teens who used social media mainly to message close friends reported higher feelings of belonging (mean 4.1 out of 5) than teens who mostly scrolled through other people's posts (mean 3.2 out of 5). Passive scrolling was linked to lower self-rated happiness.

e-schoolstart.title: Develop and justify an argument about whether high schools should start later in the morning.
e-schoolstart.label: Practice sources from Phineas's AP Psych kit, summarized and simplified.

blocks.p: When a school district in Seattle, Washington, moved high school start times from 7:50 to 8:45 a.m., students wore activity trackers before and after the change. Students slept an average of 34 minutes longer per night after the change, and median grades in biology rose by 4.5%. Absences in first period also decreased.

Researchers measured melatonin in the saliva of 120 teens ages 14–17 in Rhode Island. Melatonin, which signals the body to sleep, did not begin rising until about 10:45 p.m. on average, compared with about 9:30 p.m. for adults ages 30–45. Teens who had to wake before 6:30 a.m. scored worse on a reaction-time test.

blocks.h: Source 3: Start Times and Car Crashes
blocks.p: In two Kentucky counties, one county delayed its high school start time by one hour while a similar county did not. In the county that delayed, car crashes involving teen drivers dropped by 16.5% over two years, while crashes in the comparison county rose by 7.8%.

e-exercise.title: Develop and justify an argument about whether exercise should be recommended as a treatment for depression.
e-exercise.label: Practice sources from Phineas's AP Psych kit, summarized and simplified.

blocks.p: 156 adults ages 50–77 with major depressive disorder in North Carolina were randomly assigned to aerobic exercise (3 times a week), an antidepressant, or both for 16 weeks. All three groups improved similarly: about 60–69% no longer met criteria for depression. Six months later, the exercise-only group had a lower relapse rate (8%) than the medication-only group (38%).

In a study of 40 young adults, 30 minutes of moderate cycling increased levels of BDNF, a protein that helps neurons grow, by 32% compared with resting. Participants also reported a 25% improvement in mood ratings immediately afterward.

A review of 40 exercise studies for depression found that about 18% of participants dropped out, similar to dropout rates for antidepressant medication studies. Participants who exercised in supervised groups were less likely to drop out than those who exercised alone.

e-phones.title: Develop and justify an argument about whether schools should ban phones during class.
e-phones.label: Practice sources from Phineas's AP Psych kit, summarized and simplified.

blocks.h: Source 1: Phone Bans and Test Scores
blocks.p: Researchers studied 91 high schools in England before and after they banned phones. After the bans, students' test scores rose by an average of 6.4%, with the lowest-achieving students improving the most (14.2%).
145 college students were randomly assigned to text during a 20-minute video lecture or not. On a quiz afterward, students who texted scored 60% on average while students who did not text scored 72%.

In a survey of 2,000 students ages 13–18, 58% said they used their phones during free time at school to talk with friends, and students reported feeling more connected when they could message friends at lunch. Students who used phones only at lunch did not have lower grades than those who never used phones.

e-mindful.title: Develop and justify an argument about whether schools should teach mindfulness to reduce student stress.
e-mindful.label: Practice sources from Phineas's AP Psych kit, summarized and simplified.

blocks.p: 300 middle school students in Boston were randomly assigned to 8 weeks of mindfulness lessons or coding lessons. The mindfulness group reported 18% lower stress and had lower cortisol levels at the end of the program, while the coding group showed no change.

Undergraduates who completed 2 weeks of daily mindfulness practice improved their reading comprehension scores by 16 percentile points on a standardized test and reported less mind-wandering during the test than students in a nutrition class.

A study of 8,376 students ages 11–16 in 84 schools in the United Kingdom found that a school-based mindfulness program did not improve students' depression or well-being scores compared with usual social-emotional lessons after one year. Many students reported not practicing outside class.

e-violentgames.title: Develop and justify an argument about whether violent video games increase aggression in young people.
e-violentgames.label: Practice sources from Phineas's AP Psych kit, summarized and simplified.

blocks.h: Source 1: Short-Term Aggression in the Lab
blocks.p: 210 college students were randomly assigned to play a violent or nonviolent video game for 15 minutes. Afterward, those who played the violent game gave an opponent louder noise blasts (a lab measure of aggression) on average, 6.8 vs. 5.6 on a 10-point scale.

Researchers followed 3,034 children and teens in Singapore for 2 years. Those who played more violent games at the start reported more aggressive thoughts and behaviors two years later, even after controlling for their earlier aggression (r = +.15).

A meta-analysis combining 24 long-term studies with 17,000 participants found a small link between violent game play and later physical aggression (effect size r = .08). The researchers concluded the effect is real but small.

e-studying.title: Develop and justify an argument about the most effective way for students to study for exams.
e-studying.label: Practice sources from Phineas's AP Psych kit, summarized and simplified.

blocks.p: 120 undergraduates studied a passage either by rereading it four times or by reading it once and taking three practice recall tests. One week later, the practice-test group remembered 61% of the information compared with 40% for the rereading group.
Students who studied vocabulary in three sessions spread one week apart recalled 74% of the words on a final test, while students who studied for the same total time in one session recalled 51%.

In a survey of 177 college students, 84% said rereading notes was their main study strategy, and only 11% regularly tested themselves. Students who reported cramming the night before had lower GPAs on average (2.9) than students who spread out studying (3.3).

e-caffeineteen.title: Develop and justify an argument about whether teenagers should limit caffeine.
e-caffeineteen.label: Practice sources from Phineas's AP Psych kit, summarized and simplified.

blocks.p: Researchers tracked 1,800 teens in Canada for one week. Teens who had more than 100 mg of caffeine a day (about 1 energy drink) slept 46 minutes less on school nights than teens who had none, and were more likely to report daytime sleepiness.

In a study of 245 teens who regularly drank caffeine, 76% reported at least one withdrawal symptom, such as headaches or irritability, when they went a day without it. Teens needed more caffeine over time to feel the same alertness.

120 college students were randomly assigned to drink coffee with 200 mg of caffeine or decaf before a 30-minute attention test. The caffeine group made 18% fewer errors, but the difference disappeared for students who were already well-rested.

e-pets.title: Develop and justify an argument about whether colleges should offer therapy animal programs to reduce student stress.
e-pets.label: Practice sources from Phineas's AP Psych kit, summarized and simplified.

blocks.p: 246 undergraduates were randomly assigned to pet therapy dogs for 10 minutes, watch a slideshow of dogs, or wait. The petting group had significantly lower salivary cortisol afterward, while the other groups did not.

In an 8-week study of 300 college students at risk for academic problems, those who spent time with therapy dogs weekly showed greater improvements in executive function (planning and memory) than students who only attended stress management lectures.

A survey of 50 universities with therapy animal programs found that 92% of attending students said the program reduced their stress, but 6% of students reported avoiding events because of allergies or fear of dogs.

e-gratitude.title: Develop and justify an argument about whether writing gratitude letters improves mental health.
e-gratitude.label: Practice sources from Phineas's AP Psych kit, summarized and simplified.

blocks.p: 293 adults seeking counseling were randomly assigned to write a gratitude letter each week for 3 weeks, write about negative experiences, or do no writing. Twelve weeks later, the gratitude group reported significantly better mental health than both other groups.
In a study of 401 adults, people who scored higher on a gratitude questionnaire fell asleep faster and slept longer (r = +.29). People who were grateful had fewer negative thoughts before sleep.

A meta-analysis of 38 studies found that gratitude exercises had only a small effect on depression (d = 0.13). Effects were larger for people who did the exercises voluntarily rather than because they were assigned to.

e-teletherapy.title: Develop and justify an argument about whether online therapy is as effective as in-person therapy.
e-teletherapy.label: Practice sources from Phineas's AP Psych kit, summarized and simplified.

blocks.p: A study of 1,200 adults in Australia randomly assigned people with depression to 8 weeks of online CBT or face-to-face CBT. Both groups showed similar reductions in depression scores (about 45% average improvement).
Clients in video therapy rated their bond with their therapist at 4.3 out of 5, compared with 4.5 for in-person clients. The difference was not statistically significant.

After a rural clinic in Montana began offering video therapy, the number of patients who completed at least 8 sessions rose from 41% to 63%, mostly because patients no longer had to drive long distances.

e-medvsCBT.title: Develop and justify an argument about whether depression should be treated with medication, therapy, or both.
e-medvsCBT.label: Practice sources from Phineas's AP Psych kit, summarized and simplified.

blocks.p: 681 adults with chronic depression were randomly assigned to an antidepressant, CBT, or both for 12 weeks. 48% improved with medication alone, 48% with therapy alone, and 73% with both.
After treatment ended, 76% of patients treated only with medication relapsed within a year, compared with 31% of patients who had received CBT.
Patients taking antidepressants reported noticeable improvement after about 4 weeks on average, while therapy patients reported noticeable improvement after about 8 weeks.

e-nature.title: Develop and justify an argument about whether spending time in nature improves mental functioning.
e-nature.label: Practice sources from Phineas's AP Psych kit, summarized and simplified.

blocks.p: 38 adults were randomly assigned to take a 50-minute walk in an arboretum or along a busy downtown street. Those who walked in nature improved their scores on a backward digit span memory test by 20%, while city walkers showed no improvement.

blocks.h: Source 2: Green Space and Mental Health
blocks.p: A study of 943,000 people in Denmark found that children who grew up with the least green space nearby had up to a 55% higher risk of developing a psychiatric disorder later in life than those with the most green space.

Participants who walked in a natural area for 90 minutes reported less rumination (repetitive negative thinking) and showed reduced activity in a brain region linked to sadness, compared with participants who walked in an urban area.

e-support.title: Develop and justify an argument about whether social relationships protect physical health.
e-support.label: Practice sources from Phineas's AP Psych kit, summarized and simplified.

blocks.p: A meta-analysis of 148 studies with 308,849 participants found that people with strong social relationships had a 50% greater likelihood of survival over the study periods than people with weak social ties.
Married couples were given small blister wounds. Couples who had a hostile discussion healed 40% more slowly than couples who had a supportive discussion.
276 adults were exposed to a cold virus. People with 6 or more types of social relationships were about 4 times less likely to develop a cold than people with 1 to 3 types.

e-kidsscreens.title: Develop and justify an argument about whether children under age 3 should have limited screen time.
e-kidsscreens.label: Practice sources from Phineas's AP Psych kit, summarized and simplified.

blocks.p: Among 893 children in Canada, each 30-minute increase in daily handheld screen time at 18 months was linked to a 49% higher risk of expressive speech delay.
Toddlers ages 12–25 months learned new words from a person over live video chat as well as from a person in the room, but learned almost no words from a prerecorded video showing the same person.
Researchers recorded 329 families at home. For every extra hour of TV on in the background, adults spoke about 770 fewer words to their toddler.

e-adhdmove.title: Develop and justify an argument about whether schools should add physical activity breaks to help students with ADHD.
e-adhdmove.label: Practice sources from Phineas's AP Psych kit, summarized and simplified.

blocks.p: 54 elementary students with ADHD were randomly assigned to movement breaks or quiet reading breaks. Students with movement breaks were on task 79% of the time compared with 62% for reading breaks.
In a brain imaging study of 24 adults, 30 minutes of aerobic exercise increased the availability of dopamine in brain regions involved in attention.

202 children ages 6–8 in Vermont and Indiana did 31 minutes of activity before school for 12 weeks. Children with ADHD symptoms showed a 23% greater reduction in inattention ratings from parents than children in a sedentary program.

e-placebo.title: Develop and justify an argument about whether expectations can change how people feel physically.
e-placebo.label: Practice sources from Phineas's AP Psych kit, summarized and simplified.

blocks.p: 60 students had a heat stimulus applied to their arm after receiving an inactive cream. Those told it was a powerful pain reliever rated pain at 4.1 out of 10, while those told it was a moisturizer rated it 6.3.
97 adults with chronic back pain took pills they were told were placebos. After 3 weeks, their pain decreased by 30% compared with 9% for patients who continued usual care.
Participants who were told a fake painkiller cost $2.50 a pill reported pain relief 85% of the time, compared with 61% for those told it cost 10 cents.

e-stressimmune.title: Develop and justify an argument about whether chronic stress makes people more likely to get sick.
e-stressimmune.label: Practice sources from Phineas's AP Psych kit, summarized and simplified.

blocks.p: 276 adults were exposed to a cold virus. People who had experienced chronic stress for at least a month were 2 to 3 times more likely to develop a cold than people with no chronic stress.
Medical students' blood was tested during a calm period and during exams. During exams, their natural killer cells (immune cells that fight viruses) were 25% less active.
Adults caring for a family member with dementia took 24% longer to heal a small wound than similar adults who were not caregivers.

e-naps.title: Develop and justify an argument about whether schools should give students time for short naps.
e-naps.label: Practice sources from Phineas's AP Psych kit, summarized and simplified.

blocks.p: Students who learned 50 word pairs and then took a 60-minute nap recalled 78% of them later, compared with 63% for students who stayed awake.
A 10-minute nap improved alertness and reaction time for 2.5 hours in sleep-deprived adults, while a 30-minute nap caused grogginess for about 15 minutes afterward.

A survey of 2,928 students ages 10–12 in China, where midday naps are common, found that students who napped 3 or more times a week had 7.6% higher academic achievement scores and fewer behavior problems.

e-concussion.title: Develop and justify an argument about whether children under 12 should play tackle football.
e-concussion.label: Practice sources from Phineas's AP Psych kit, summarized and simplified.

blocks.p: Among 214 former football players, those who began tackle football before age 12 had twice the risk of problems with behavior and mood later in life as those who started at 12 or older.

blocks.h: Source 2: Head Impacts in Youth Players
blocks.p: Sensors in helmets of 9- to 12-year-old players recorded an average of 240 head impacts per season, and some impacts were as forceful as those in college football.
In a survey of 11,000 adolescents, those who played team sports had 19% lower odds of depression symptoms than those who did not play any sport.

e-rewards.title: Develop and justify an argument about whether schools should give students rewards for reading books.
e-rewards.label: Practice sources from Phineas's AP Psych kit, summarized and simplified.

blocks.p: In a program across 2,500 elementary schools, students earned a free pizza for reading a set number of books. During the 6-month program, students in participating classes read an average of 8 more books than students in non-participating classes.

Researchers followed 160 fourth graders after a 4-week reading reward program ended. Students who had been rewarded chose to read during free time 22% of the time afterward, compared with 41% for similar students who had never been rewarded.

In a study of 1,100 middle school students in Texas, students who were allowed to choose their own books reported enjoying reading 1.5 times more than students assigned books, and read for 15 more minutes per day at home.

e-allnighter.title: Develop and justify an argument about whether students should stay up all night to study before a test.
e-allnighter.label: Practice sources from Phineas's AP Psych kit, summarized and simplified.

blocks.p: 28 young adults either slept normally or stayed awake for 35 hours, then tried to learn 150 pictures. The sleep-deprived group remembered 19% fewer pictures two days later than the group that slept.

blocks.h: Source 2: Students Who Never Pulled All-Nighters
blocks.p: In a survey of 120 students at a college in New York, students who had pulled at least one all-nighter that semester had an average GPA of 2.95, compared with 3.1 for students who never had.
After 24 hours without sleep, 40 adults performed on a driving simulator about as poorly as people with a blood alcohol level of 0.10%, which is above the legal limit for driving.

e-praise.title: Develop and justify an argument about how parents and teachers should praise children.
e-praise.label: Practice sources from Phineas's AP Psych kit, summarized and simplified.

blocks.p: 128 fifth graders solved puzzles and were randomly praised either for being smart or for working hard. When given a harder puzzle afterward, 90% of the effort-praised children chose a challenging task, compared with about 33% of the intelligence-praised children.

Researchers recorded parents talking with their 1- to 3-year-olds at home and followed the children for 5 years. Children whose parents gave more effort praise were more likely at ages 7–8 to believe that abilities can improve with practice (r = +.32).

A 50-minute online lesson teaching that the brain can grow with effort was given to 12,000 ninth graders in the U.S. Lower-achieving students who took the lesson raised their GPAs by 0.10 points more than students who did not.

e-music.title: Develop and justify an argument about whether students should listen to music while studying.
e-music.label: Practice sources from Phineas's AP Psych kit, summarized and simplified.

blocks.p: 64 college students read passages in silence, with instrumental music, or with music that had lyrics. Students reading with lyrical music scored 18% lower on comprehension than those in silence; instrumental music did not significantly lower scores.
In a survey of 500 high school students, 72% said music helped them feel less bored while doing homework, and students who listened to music they liked reported starting homework sooner.
Participants who memorized lists of letters while listening to music they liked recalled 11% fewer letters than participants who worked in quiet, even though many said the music helped them.

e-teenbrain.title: Develop and justify an argument about whether the minimum age for an unrestricted driver's license should be raised to 18.
e-teenbrain.label: Practice sources from Phineas's AP Psych kit, summarized and simplified.

blocks.p: Drivers ages 16–17 in the U.S. had a crash rate about 3 times higher per mile driven than drivers age 20 and older. Crash risk was highest in the first 6 months after getting a license.

In a driving simulator study of 66 teenage drivers, teens who drove with a friend in the car ran 40% more yellow lights and took more risks than teens who drove alone. Adults' driving did not change with passengers.

States with strict graduated licensing laws (limits on night driving and teen passengers for new drivers) saw a 20% drop in fatal crashes among 16-year-old drivers compared with states without such laws.

e-loneliness.title: Develop and justify an argument about whether communities should invest in programs that connect older adults with others.
e-loneliness.label: Practice sources from Phineas's AP Psych kit, summarized and simplified.

blocks.p: A study of 3,000 adults ages 57–85 in the U.S. found that those who felt lonely had blood pressure readings an average of 14 points higher than those who did not, and were 45% more likely to die over the 6-year study.

Older adults who volunteered in elementary schools for 15 hours a week for one school year showed improved memory test scores and increased activity in brain areas linked to planning, compared with a waitlist group.
240 adults over 65 who received short, friendly phone calls 2–5 times a week for 4 weeks reported 20% less loneliness and fewer symptoms of anxiety than adults who did not receive calls.

e-marijuana.title: Develop and justify an argument about whether communities should invest in programs to prevent teenagers from using marijuana.
e-marijuana.label: Practice sources from Phineas's AP Psych kit, summarized and simplified.

blocks.p: Researchers compared 48 adolescents who used marijuana weekly with 50 non-users. The weekly users scored 12% lower on a test of verbal memory, even after not using for one month.

A study of 1,037 people in New Zealand followed from birth to age 38 found that those who used marijuana regularly starting in their teens lost an average of 8 IQ points; people who started as adults did not show the same drop.
Middle schools in Iowa that used a 7-session prevention program had 33% fewer students who tried marijuana by 12th grade than schools without the program.

e-eatingdis.title: Develop and justify an argument about whether social media platforms should limit appearance-focused content shown to teens.
e-eatingdis.label: Practice sources from Phineas's AP Psych kit, summarized and simplified.

blocks.p: 112 young women were randomly assigned to view Instagram posts of thin, edited models or posts of travel scenes for 10 minutes. Afterward, the model group's body satisfaction scores dropped by 14% while the travel group's did not change.

A survey of 1,000 girls ages 12–17 found that those who spent more than 2 hours a day on image-based apps were 2 times as likely to report disordered eating behaviors, such as skipping meals to lose weight.

Participants who viewed body-positive posts (showing a range of body types) for 10 minutes reported higher body satisfaction and appreciation for their own bodies than participants who viewed neutral posts.

e-ptsdtreat.title: Develop and justify an argument about whether exposure-based therapy should be the first treatment offered for PTSD.
e-ptsdtreat.label: Practice sources from Phineas's AP Psych kit, summarized and simplified.

blocks.p: In a study of 284 female veterans with PTSD, those who received 10 sessions of prolonged exposure therapy (repeatedly and safely revisiting trauma memories) were 1.8 times more likely to no longer meet criteria for PTSD than veterans who received supportive talk therapy.
Five years after treatment with exposure-based therapy, 78% of 171 patients with PTSD from a car accident still showed significant improvement in symptoms.
A review of 55 studies found that about 28% of patients in trauma-focused therapies dropped out, slightly higher than the 23% dropout rate for non-trauma-focused therapies.

e-bilingual.title: Develop and justify an argument about whether elementary schools should start teaching a second language in kindergarten.
e-bilingual.label: Practice sources from Phineas's AP Psych kit, summarized and simplified.

blocks.p: Researchers tested 240 immigrants who learned English at different ages. Those who began before age 7 spoke with native-like pronunciation 85% of the time, compared with 25% of those who began after age 15.

In a study of 104 children ages 5–7, bilingual children scored 15% higher than monolingual children on tasks that required switching between rules, such as sorting cards first by color and then by shape.

blocks.h: Source 3: Language Programs and Test Scores
blocks.p: In North Carolina, students in dual-language programs that began in kindergarten scored about half a grade level higher in reading by 5th grade than similar students in English-only classes.

parts.prompt: Propose a specific and defensible claim based in psychological science that responds to the question.
parts.model: Adolescents should limit daily social media use, especially passive scrolling, to reduce symptoms of depression and loneliness.

parts.prompt: Support your claim using at least one piece of specific and relevant evidence from one of the sources.
parts.model: Students who limited their social media use to 30 minutes per day showed significant reductions in loneliness and depression compared with the control group (Source 1).

parts.prompt: Explain how the evidence from Part B(i) supports your claim using a psychological perspective, theory, concept, or research finding learned in AP Psychology.
parts.model: This supports the claim because cutting time on social media directly reduced negative feelings. This can be explained by social comparison theory: when adolescents spend less time viewing curated posts from peers, they make fewer upward social comparisons, which reduces feelings of inadequacy and depressive symptoms.

parts.prompt: Support your claim using an additional piece of specific and relevant evidence from a different source than the one that you used to support your claim in Part B(i).
parts.model: Teens who mostly scrolled through other people's posts reported lower belonging (3.2 out of 5) than teens who mainly messaged close friends (4.1 out of 5) (Source 3).

parts.prompt: Explain how the evidence from Part C(i) supports your claim using a different psychological perspective, theory, concept, or research finding learned in AP Psychology than the one that you used in Part B(ii).
parts.model: This supports limiting passive use because scrolling, rather than connecting, was tied to lower belonging and happiness. According to Maslow's hierarchy of needs, belongingness is a basic need that must be met before self-esteem and growth; passive scrolling fails to satisfy this need, so limiting it frees time for real connection that meets it.

parts.prompt: Propose a specific and defensible claim based in psychological science that responds to the question.
parts.model: High schools should start later in the morning because a later start lets teens get more sleep, which improves their grades and safety.

parts.prompt: Support your claim using at least one piece of specific and relevant evidence from one of the sources.
parts.model: After Seattle high schools moved start times from 7:50 to 8:45 a.m., students slept 34 minutes longer and median biology grades rose by 4.5% (Source 1).

parts.prompt: Explain how the evidence from Part B(i) supports your claim using a psychological perspective, theory, concept, or research finding learned in AP Psychology.
parts.model: This supports the claim because the extra sleep from the later start was followed by better academic performance. This can be explained by memory consolidation: during sleep, the brain moves newly learned information into long-term memory, so students who sleep longer can store and recall more of what they learned in class.

parts.prompt: Support your claim using an additional piece of specific and relevant evidence from a different source than the one that you used to support your claim in Part B(i).
parts.model: Teens' melatonin did not begin rising until about 10:45 p.m., compared with about 9:30 p.m. for adults (Source 2).

parts.prompt: Explain how the evidence from Part C(i) supports your claim using a different psychological perspective, theory, concept, or research finding learned in AP Psychology than the one that you used in Part B(ii).
parts.model: This supports a later start because teens are not able to fall asleep early, so an early start cuts their sleep short. This is explained by the circadian rhythm: during adolescence the biological clock shifts later, so teens are naturally evening-energized, and forcing them to wake early works against their internal 24-hour cycle.

parts.prompt: Propose a specific and defensible claim based in psychological science that responds to the question.
parts.model: Exercise should be recommended as a treatment for depression because it reduces symptoms about as well as medication and helps prevent relapse.

parts.prompt: Support your claim using at least one piece of specific and relevant evidence from one of the sources.
parts.model: Six months after treatment, adults who only exercised had a relapse rate of 8%, compared with 38% for those who only took medication (Source 1).

parts.prompt: Explain how the evidence from Part B(i) supports your claim using a psychological perspective, theory, concept, or research finding learned in AP Psychology.
parts.model: This supports the claim because exercise not only reduced depression but kept it from coming back better than medication. From the behavioral perspective, exercise works through positive reinforcement: the mood boost after each workout rewards the behavior, making people more likely to keep exercising, which sustains the improvement.

parts.prompt: Support your claim using an additional piece of specific and relevant evidence from a different source than the one that you used to support your claim in Part B(i).
parts.model: Thirty minutes of moderate cycling raised mood ratings by 25% right afterward (Source 2).

parts.prompt: Explain how the evidence from Part C(i) supports your claim using a different psychological perspective, theory, concept, or research finding learned in AP Psychology than the one that you used in Part B(ii).
parts.model: This supports recommending exercise because even one session improved mood. This can be explained by endorphins, the brain's natural painkillers that are released during exercise; they produce positive feelings (a "runner's high") that counteract the low mood of depression.

parts.prompt: Propose a specific and defensible claim based in psychological science that responds to the question.
parts.model: Schools should ban phones during class time because phones distract students and lower their learning.

parts.prompt: Support your claim using at least one piece of specific and relevant evidence from one of the sources.
parts.model: After 91 high schools in England banned phones, students' test scores rose by 6.4% on average, and the lowest-achieving students improved by 14.2% (Source 1).

parts.prompt: Explain how the evidence from Part B(i) supports your claim using a psychological perspective, theory, concept, or research finding learned in AP Psychology.
parts.model: This supports the claim because removing phones was followed by higher achievement. This can be explained by selective attention: we can only focus our conscious awareness on a limited amount at once, so a phone pulls attention away from the lesson, and removing it lets students focus fully on what is being taught.

parts.prompt: Support your claim using an additional piece of specific and relevant evidence from a different source than the one that you used to support your claim in Part B(i).
parts.model: Students who texted during a lecture scored 60% on a quiz, compared with 72% for students who did not text (Source 2).

parts.prompt: Explain how the evidence from Part C(i) supports your claim using a different psychological perspective, theory, concept, or research finding learned in AP Psychology than the one that you used in Part B(ii).
parts.model: This supports a ban during class because texting directly reduced how much students learned. This is explained by encoding: to remember information, it must first be encoded into memory, and dividing attention between texting and the lecture means less of the lecture is encoded into long-term memory.

parts.prompt: Propose a specific and defensible claim based in psychological science that responds to the question.
parts.model: Schools should teach mindfulness because it reduces students' stress and improves their focus, especially when students actually practice it.

parts.prompt: Support your claim using at least one piece of specific and relevant evidence from one of the sources.
parts.model: Middle school students who took 8 weeks of mindfulness lessons reported 18% lower stress and had lower cortisol levels, while students in coding lessons showed no change (Source 1).

parts.prompt: Explain how the evidence from Part B(i) supports your claim using a psychological perspective, theory, concept, or research finding learned in AP Psychology.
parts.model: This supports the claim because mindfulness lowered both reported stress and a biological stress marker. This can be explained by the parasympathetic nervous system: mindful breathing activates the rest-and-digest response, calming the body after the sympathetic fight-or-flight response, which lowers stress hormones.

parts.prompt: Support your claim using an additional piece of specific and relevant evidence from a different source than the one that you used to support your claim in Part B(i).
parts.model: Undergraduates who practiced mindfulness daily for 2 weeks improved their reading comprehension by 16 percentile points and reported less mind-wandering (Source 2).

parts.prompt: Explain how the evidence from Part C(i) supports your claim using a different psychological perspective, theory, concept, or research finding learned in AP Psychology than the one that you used in Part B(ii).
parts.model: This supports teaching mindfulness because it helped students focus during a test. This is explained by emotion-focused coping: mindfulness helps students regulate anxious feelings about a stressor instead of being overwhelmed by them, so they can direct attention back to the task.

parts.prompt: Propose a specific and defensible claim based in psychological science that responds to the question.
parts.model: Violent video games slightly increase aggression in young people, so parents should limit how much violent gaming children do.

parts.prompt: Support your claim using at least one piece of specific and relevant evidence from one of the sources.
parts.model: College students who played a violent game for 15 minutes gave louder noise blasts to an opponent than students who played a nonviolent game, 6.8 versus 5.6 on a 10-point scale (Source 1).

parts.prompt: Explain how the evidence from Part B(i) supports your claim using a psychological perspective, theory, concept, or research finding learned in AP Psychology.
parts.model: This supports the claim because playing a violent game caused more aggressive behavior right afterward in an experiment. This can be explained by observational learning: players watch and imitate aggressive models in the game, much like children in Bandura's Bobo doll study imitated an adult who hit the doll, which makes aggressive responses more likely.

parts.prompt: Support your claim using an additional piece of specific and relevant evidence from a different source than the one that you used to support your claim in Part B(i).
parts.model: A meta-analysis of 24 studies with 17,000 participants found a small but real link between violent game play and later physical aggression (r = .08) (Source 3).

parts.prompt: Explain how the evidence from Part C(i) supports your claim using a different psychological perspective, theory, concept, or research finding learned in AP Psychology than the one that you used in Part B(ii).
parts.model: This supports the claim that the increase is slight because combining many studies shows a consistent but small effect. From the behavioral perspective, games reward violent actions with points and progress, so through operant conditioning (positive reinforcement) players learn that aggression pays off, even if the effect on real behavior is modest.

parts.prompt: Propose a specific and defensible claim based in psychological science that responds to the question.
parts.model: The most effective way to study is to quiz yourself on material over several spaced-out sessions instead of rereading or cramming.

parts.prompt: Support your claim using at least one piece of specific and relevant evidence from one of the sources.
parts.model: Students who took practice recall tests remembered 61% of a passage after one week, compared with 40% for students who reread it four times (Source 1).

parts.prompt: Explain how the evidence from Part B(i) supports your claim using a psychological perspective, theory, concept, or research finding learned in AP Psychology.
parts.model: This supports the claim because self-quizzing led to much better long-term memory than rereading. This is explained by the testing effect: actively retrieving information strengthens the memory pathways for it, so each practice test makes the information easier to recall later.

parts.prompt: Support your claim using an additional piece of specific and relevant evidence from a different source than the one that you used to support your claim in Part B(i).
parts.model: Students who studied vocabulary in three sessions a week apart recalled 74% of the words, compared with 51% for students who studied for the same time in one session (Source 2).

parts.prompt: Explain how the evidence from Part C(i) supports your claim using a different psychological perspective, theory, concept, or research finding learned in AP Psychology than the one that you used in Part B(ii).
parts.model: This supports spacing out study sessions because spacing improved recall by more than 20 percentage points. This is explained by the spacing effect (distributed practice): information studied over time is consolidated more strongly into long-term memory than information crammed in one session (massed practice).

parts.prompt: Propose a specific and defensible claim based in psychological science that responds to the question.
parts.model: Teenagers should limit caffeine because it cuts into their sleep and can lead to dependence.

parts.prompt: Support your claim using at least one piece of specific and relevant evidence from one of the sources.
parts.model: Teens who had more than 100 mg of caffeine a day slept 46 minutes less on school nights than teens who had none (Source 1).

parts.prompt: Explain how the evidence from Part B(i) supports your claim using a psychological perspective, theory, concept, or research finding learned in AP Psychology.
parts.model: This supports the claim because caffeine was linked to losing nearly an hour of sleep a night. Caffeine is a stimulant that excites the central nervous system; this explains why it interferes with falling asleep and disrupts the circadian rhythm's normal signal to sleep at night.

parts.prompt: Support your claim using an additional piece of specific and relevant evidence from a different source than the one that you used to support your claim in Part B(i).
parts.model: 76% of teens who regularly drank caffeine reported withdrawal symptoms such as headaches or irritability when they went a day without it (Source 2).

parts.prompt: Explain how the evidence from Part C(i) supports your claim using a different psychological perspective, theory, concept, or research finding learned in AP Psychology than the one that you used in Part B(ii).
parts.model: This supports limiting caffeine because many teens are already physically dependent on it. This is explained by tolerance and withdrawal: with regular use the body adapts, so teens need more caffeine for the same effect, and stopping causes discomfort, which keeps them using it.

parts.prompt: Propose a specific and defensible claim based in psychological science that responds to the question.
parts.model: Colleges should offer therapy animal programs because interacting with animals reduces students' stress and helps them think more clearly.

parts.prompt: Support your claim using at least one piece of specific and relevant evidence from one of the sources.
parts.model: Students who petted therapy dogs for 10 minutes had significantly lower cortisol afterward, while students who watched a slideshow of dogs or waited did not (Source 1).

parts.prompt: Explain how the evidence from Part B(i) supports your claim using a psychological perspective, theory, concept, or research finding learned in AP Psychology.
parts.model: This supports the claim because touching a real animal lowered a biological stress marker. This connects to the General Adaptation Syndrome: chronic stress keeps students in the resistance stage with stress hormones flowing, and a calming activity can lower cortisol before they reach the exhaustion stage.

parts.prompt: Support your claim using an additional piece of specific and relevant evidence from a different source than the one that you used to support your claim in Part B(i).
parts.model: Students at risk for academic problems who spent time with therapy dogs every week for 8 weeks improved more in planning and memory than students who attended stress lectures (Source 2).

parts.prompt: Explain how the evidence from Part C(i) supports your claim using a different psychological perspective, theory, concept, or research finding learned in AP Psychology than the one that you used in Part B(ii).
parts.model: This supports the claim because lower stress was linked to better thinking skills. This can be explained by the prefrontal cortex, which handles planning, judgment, and decision making; high stress impairs it, so reducing stress lets it function better.

parts.prompt: Propose a specific and defensible claim based in psychological science that responds to the question.
parts.model: Writing gratitude letters improves mental health, but the benefits are modest and strongest for people who choose to do it.

parts.prompt: Support your claim using at least one piece of specific and relevant evidence from one of the sources.
parts.model: Adults who wrote a weekly gratitude letter for 3 weeks reported better mental health 12 weeks later than adults who wrote about negative experiences or did no writing (Source 1).

parts.prompt: Explain how the evidence from Part B(i) supports your claim using a psychological perspective, theory, concept, or research finding learned in AP Psychology.
parts.model: This supports the claim because gratitude writing had a lasting positive effect on mental health. This can be explained by cognitive restructuring: focusing on positive events replaces automatic negative thoughts with more positive, realistic ones, which improves mood over time.

parts.prompt: Support your claim using an additional piece of specific and relevant evidence from a different source than the one that you used to support your claim in Part B(i).
parts.model: A meta-analysis of 38 studies found gratitude exercises had only a small effect on depression (d = 0.13), with larger effects for people who did them voluntarily (Source 3).

parts.prompt: Explain how the evidence from Part C(i) supports your claim using a different psychological perspective, theory, concept, or research finding learned in AP Psychology than the one that you used in Part B(ii).
parts.model: This supports the claim that benefits are modest and depend on choice. This is explained by intrinsic motivation: people who do an activity because they want to engage with it more deeply and get more out of it than people pushed by outside requirements.

parts.prompt: Propose a specific and defensible claim based in psychological science that responds to the question.
parts.model: Online therapy is as effective as in-person therapy and should be offered because it helps more people complete treatment.

parts.prompt: Support your claim using at least one piece of specific and relevant evidence from one of the sources.
parts.model: Adults with depression who received 8 weeks of online CBT improved by about 45%, the same as adults who received face-to-face CBT (Source 1).

parts.prompt: Explain how the evidence from Part B(i) supports your claim using a psychological perspective, theory, concept, or research finding learned in AP Psychology.
parts.model: This supports the claim because both formats produced the same improvement. CBT works by cognitive restructuring, helping clients identify and replace negative thoughts; this process depends on what is taught and practiced, not on being in the same room, so it works just as well online.

parts.prompt: Support your claim using an additional piece of specific and relevant evidence from a different source than the one that you used to support your claim in Part B(i).
parts.model: After a rural clinic offered video therapy, the share of patients completing at least 8 sessions rose from 41% to 63% (Source 3).

parts.prompt: Explain how the evidence from Part C(i) supports your claim using a different psychological perspective, theory, concept, or research finding learned in AP Psychology than the one that you used in Part B(ii).
parts.model: This supports offering online therapy because more people finished treatment when it was easier to attend. From the humanistic perspective, therapy helps people reach their full potential through a supportive relationship, and removing barriers lets more people experience the unconditional positive regard that drives growth.

parts.prompt: Propose a specific and defensible claim based in psychological science that responds to the question.
parts.model: Depression should be treated with both medication and therapy because the combination helps the most people improve.

parts.prompt: Support your claim using at least one piece of specific and relevant evidence from one of the sources.
parts.model: After 12 weeks, 73% of adults with chronic depression improved with both medication and CBT, compared with 48% with either one alone (Source 1).

parts.prompt: Explain how the evidence from Part B(i) supports your claim using a psychological perspective, theory, concept, or research finding learned in AP Psychology.
parts.model: This supports the claim because combining treatments helped far more patients. This fits the biopsychosocial model: depression involves biological factors (like serotonin imbalances that antidepressants target) and psychological factors (like negative thinking that therapy targets), so treating both works best.

parts.prompt: Support your claim using an additional piece of specific and relevant evidence from a different source than the one that you used to support your claim in Part B(i).
parts.model: 76% of patients treated only with medication relapsed within a year, compared with 31% of patients who had received CBT (Source 2).

parts.prompt: Explain how the evidence from Part C(i) supports your claim using a different psychological perspective, theory, concept, or research finding learned in AP Psychology than the one that you used in Part B(ii).
parts.model: This supports including therapy because therapy gave patients lasting protection. Aaron Beck's cognitive theory explains this: CBT teaches patients to recognize and challenge the negative cognitive triad (negative thoughts about the self, world, and future), a skill that keeps working after treatment ends.

parts.prompt: Propose a specific and defensible claim based in psychological science that responds to the question.
parts.model: Spending time in nature improves mental functioning by restoring attention and reducing negative thinking.

parts.prompt: Support your claim using at least one piece of specific and relevant evidence from one of the sources.

parts.prompt: Explain how the evidence from Part B(i) supports your claim using a psychological perspective, theory, concept, or research finding learned in AP Psychology.

parts.model: This supports the claim because nature reduced repetitive negative thinking. Selective attention explains this: in nature, attention is gently drawn outward to the surroundings instead of focusing on one's own worries, which interrupts the cycle of rumination.

parts.prompt: Support your claim using at least one piece of specific and relevant evidence from one of the sources.

parts.model: This supports the claim because more relationships meant better resistance to illness. This is explained by the tend-and-befriend response: under stress, seeking out social support calms the body's stress reaction, reducing stress hormones that otherwise cause immunosuppression.

sections.name: Timed AAQ (25 min)

guide.p: 7 points · 25 minutes (including a 10-minute reading period) · 1 summarized peer-reviewed article. Parts A–E are 1 point each; Part F is 2.

table: Look for random assignment, manipulation of a variable, and control/experimental groups.
Scan the Method section for how the variable was actually measured or tested.
Always connect the number back to what it means for the research question.
Read the Method section carefully. Ethical practices are often described without being named.
The demographic table is the key. Reference specific percentages from the participant data.
Use specific numbers from the Results section and explicitly say whether they support or refute the hypothesis.

rows: Identify
Name it. No explanation needed. One sentence is enough.
Describe
Give the relevant characteristics: what it is and what it shows. You don't need to explain why.
Explain
The big one: HOW or WHY something happens, with evidence and reasoning.

guide.p: You can't write, but you CAN annotate. 1) First read (3–4 min): what were they studying, what did they find? 2) Annotate (4–5 min): method, IV and DV, operational definitions, statistics, ethical practices, demographics. 3) Preview the six questions (1–2 min).

Reading 10 min · Parts A–D about 7 min (~1.5 each) · Parts E–F about 8 min (3–4 each). Never spend more than 2 minutes on a 1-point part. Save 3–4 minutes for Part F. If you finish early, recheck E and F first: that's where most points are lost.

Label every part (A, B, C…). Answer what's asked: match the task verb. Use psych terminology ("randomly assigned to experimental and control conditions," not "split into groups"). Quote the article: numbers, percentages, details.

examTips: Turn the Timer on. The real AAQ is 25 minutes, including a 10-minute reading period.
Answer every part, then press Check my answers on each article.

a-sleep.title: Sleep Deprivation and Memory for Word Lists
a-sleep.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-sleep.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: Researchers wanted to know whether losing a night of sleep affects how well people remember new information. They hypothesized that sleep deprivation impairs memory.
120 undergraduate students from a single university in Ohio took part in exchange for course credit. Participants were 18 to 22 years old (mean age 19.6). See the table for demographics.

Participants were randomly assigned to one of two groups. The sleep-deprived group stayed awake all night in the sleep lab, monitored by research assistants. The rested group slept for 8 hours in the same lab. The next morning, every participant studied a list of 40 words for 5 minutes and then had 3 minutes to write down as many of the words as they could remember. Memory recall was measured as the number of words correctly written down. Before the study, every participant read and signed a consent form that explained they might be asked to stay awake all night. They were told they could leave the study at any time without losing their course credit. After the study, all participants were debriefed about the purpose of the research.

The rested group recalled an average of 18.4 words (SD = 4.1). The sleep-deprived group recalled an average of 12.7 words (SD = 4.6). This difference was statistically significant (p < .001), and the effect size was large (d = 1.31).

Participants who missed a night of sleep remembered about 6 fewer words than participants who slept. The researchers note that the sample included only college students and that future research should include other age groups.

a-naps.title: Afternoon Naps and Memory Consolidation
a-naps.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-naps.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: Researchers tested the hypothesis that a short afternoon nap helps people hold on to newly learned information.
64 university students in Germany took part. Participants were 19 to 28 years old (mean age 22.9). See the table for demographics.

All participants learned 50 pairs of words at noon. They were then randomly assigned to take a 60-minute nap in the lab or to watch a nature video for 60 minutes while staying awake. At 5 p.m., memory was measured as the percentage of word pairs participants correctly recalled when shown the first word of each pair. Participants gave informed consent and were told they could leave at any time.
The nap group recalled 78% of word pairs on average. The video group recalled 63% (p < .001).
A short nap helped participants retain new information. The researchers note that all participants were university students in one country.

a-mindset.title: Growth Mindset Lessons and Math Grades
a-mindset.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-mindset.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: A growth mindset is the belief that abilities can improve with effort. Researchers tested the hypothesis that a short growth mindset program raises math grades.
1,200 ninth graders from 10 public high schools in North Carolina took part. Students were 14 to 15 years old. See the table for demographics.

Students were randomly assigned to complete two 25-minute online lessons about how the brain grows with effort (growth mindset) or two 25-minute lessons about brain functions (control). Math achievement was measured as each student's end-of-year math grade point average on a 4.0 scale. Parents were notified and could opt their child out, and students' records were analyzed without names.
Growth mindset students finished the year with an average math GPA of 2.48; control students averaged 2.39 (p = .03). The effect size was small (d = 0.10).
The program produced a small but statistically significant improvement in math grades.

a-lithium.title: Lithium and Relapse in Bipolar Disorder
a-lithium.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-lithium.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: Mood stabilizers such as lithium are used to treat bipolar disorder. Researchers tested the hypothesis that lithium prevents mood episodes better than a placebo.
180 adults with bipolar I disorder from hospitals in the United Kingdom took part. Participants were 21 to 65 years old (mean age 42.0). See the table for demographics.

All participants were currently stable. They were randomly assigned to take lithium or an identical placebo pill daily for 18 months, in a double-blind design. Relapse was measured as having a manic or depressive episode severe enough to need a change in treatment, as decided by a psychiatrist. Participants gave informed consent, their blood was checked monthly for safe lithium levels, and anyone who relapsed was immediately given full treatment.
By 18 months, 31% of the lithium group had relapsed, compared with 63% of the placebo group (p < .001).
Lithium cut the relapse rate roughly in half.

a-groupdep.title: Group vs. Individual Therapy for Depression
a-groupdep.attr: Adapted summary of a peer-reviewed study (practice article written for this kit).
a-groupdep.label: Practice article from Phineas's AP Psych kit (a fictional study written for practice).

blocks.p: Researchers tested the hypothesis that group therapy is as effective as individual therapy for depression.
160 adults with major depressive disorder from community clinics in Ontario, Canada, took part. Participants were 20 to 65 years old (mean age 40.7). See the table for demographics.

Participants were randomly assigned to 12 weeks of individual CBT (one therapist, one client) or group CBT (one therapist, 8 clients). Both used the same lessons. Depression was measured with the PHQ-9 (0 to 27). Cost was measured as the clinic's total therapist cost per client. Participants gave informed consent, group members agreed to keep what others shared private, and anyone at risk of self-harm received immediate individual care.

PHQ-9 scores dropped by 7.8 points in the individual group and 7.2 points in the group-therapy group. The difference was not statistically significant (p = .48). Group therapy cost $420 per client, compared with $1,560 for individual therapy.
Group therapy reduced depression about as well as individual therapy at a much lower cost.

questions.title: Sleep Deprivation and Memory for Word Lists

labels: Says it was a count of words
Gives a detail from this study (the 40-word list, 3 minutes, writing them down)

parts.prompt: Identify the research method used in the study.
parts.model: The research method is an experiment because participants were randomly assigned to the sleep-deprived or rested group, and the researchers manipulated the amount of sleep (the independent variable).

parts.prompt: State the operational definition of memory recall.
parts.model: Memory recall was operationally defined as the number of words participants correctly wrote down in 3 minutes after studying a list of 40 words for 5 minutes.

parts.prompt: Describe what the difference in mean words recalled indicates about the two groups.
parts.model: The rested group recalled more words on average (18.4) than the sleep-deprived group (12.7), which indicates that participants who slept remembered more of the word list than participants who stayed awake all night.

parts.prompt: Identify one ethical guideline the researchers followed and describe how they applied it.
parts.model: The researchers followed informed consent: before the study, every participant read and signed a consent form explaining that they might have to stay awake all night.

parts.prompt: Explain the extent to which the research findings can be generalized, using specific evidence from the participants.
parts.model: The findings are limited in how far they can be generalized because all participants were 18 to 22-year-old undergraduates from one university in Ohio, and 74% were White. The results may apply to young college students but cannot be confidently extended to older adults, children, or more racially diverse populations.

parts.prompt: Explain how the results support or refute the researchers' hypothesis that sleep deprivation impairs memory.
parts.model: The results support the hypothesis that sleep deprivation impairs memory. The sleep-deprived group recalled an average of 12.7 words compared with 18.4 words for the rested group, a statistically significant difference (p < .001) with a large effect size, which shows that missing a night of sleep caused participants to remember fewer words.

Evidence: Students who limited their social media use to 30 minutes per day showed significant reductions in loneliness and depression compared to the control group (Source 1).
Explanation: This supports the claim that adolescents should reduce social media use, because spending less time on these platforms decreased negative psychological outcomes.

e-socialmedia.title: Develop and justify an argument about whether adolescents should limit their social media use.
e-socialmedia.label: Practice sources from Phineas's AP Psych kit, summarized and simplified.

blocks.p: 143 undergraduates (ages 18–22) at a university in Pennsylvania were randomly assigned to limit social media to 30 minutes per day or to use it as usual for 3 weeks. Students who limited their use showed significant reductions in loneliness and depression compared with the control group (p < .05). Those who started with higher depression scores improved the most.

blocks.h: Source 2: Screen Time and Teen Depression
blocks.p: A survey of 6,595 U.S. teens ages 12–15 found that teens who spent more than 3 hours a day on social media were twice as likely to report high levels of anxiety and depression symptoms as teens who did not use social media. The relationship remained after accounting for gender and family income. The study was correlational.

In a study of 1,200 adolescents ages 13–17 in the United Kingdom, teens who used social media mainly to message close friends reported higher feelings of belonging (mean 4.1 out of 5) than teens who mostly scrolled through other people's posts (mean 3.2 out of 5). Passive scrolling was linked to lower self-rated happiness.

e-teletherapy.title: Develop and justify an argument about whether online therapy is as effective as in-person therapy.
e-teletherapy.label: Practice sources from Phineas's AP Psych kit, summarized and simplified.

blocks.p: A study of 1,200 adults in Australia randomly assigned people with depression to 8 weeks of online CBT or face-to-face CBT. Both groups showed similar reductions in depression scores (about 45% average improvement).
Clients in video therapy rated their bond with their therapist at 4.3 out of 5, compared with 4.5 for in-person clients. The difference was not statistically significant.

After a rural clinic in Montana began offering video therapy, the number of patients who completed at least 8 sessions rose from 41% to 63%, mostly because patients no longer had to drive long distances.

e-rewards.title: Develop and justify an argument about whether schools should give students rewards for reading books.
e-rewards.label: Practice sources from Phineas's AP Psych kit, summarized and simplified.

blocks.p: In a program across 2,500 elementary schools, students earned a free pizza for reading a set number of books. During the 6-month program, students in participating classes read an average of 8 more books than students in non-participating classes.

Researchers followed 160 fourth graders after a 4-week reading reward program ended. Students who had been rewarded chose to read during free time 22% of the time afterward, compared with 41% for similar students who had never been rewarded.

In a study of 1,100 middle school students in Texas, students who were allowed to choose their own books reported enjoying reading 1.5 times more than students assigned books, and read for 15 more minutes per day at home.
